19728-northern-nut-growers-association-r:
Nut growers in the northern United States formed an association to share craft knowledge. Its reports record proceedings, papers, and member lists. One surviving page lists pomologists from the Department of Agriculture in Washington. Names like Professor C. P. Close and Walter Van Fleet appear among them. Van Fleet was a noted plant breeder of the era.

Northern nut growing faced cold winters that southern growers escaped. Chestnuts, walnuts, and hickories needed hardy strains and patient testing. Association reports spread results that no single farm could gather. They list who grew what, and where. For farm historians, such lists are gold. They show American horticulture organizing itself, name by name.
19859-a-flat-iron-for-a-farthing-or-some:
Juliana Horatia Ewing wrote A Flat Iron for a Farthing, passages in the life of an only son. When children clamor for a story, the narrator's wife sends them to him. Tell them how you bought a flat iron for a farthing, she says. He is glad to tell it for three reasons. It is about himself, someone dear, and his own childhood. The tale unfolds as family storytelling.

Ewing was among the finest Victorian writers for children. Her only son narrates with humor and exact memory. A farthing's purchase becomes an epic of childhood economy. Grown readers find real feeling under the comedy. The book influenced later masters of children's fiction. It deserves its classic standing.
20200-christmas-a-happy-time-a-tale-calc:
Christmas: A Happy Time is a tale made for the amusement of young readers. Harriet warns that some hoped-for guests will never come at last. She reminds the others not to open the gate outside. Papa and mamma have both forbidden it, she says with care.

The children shiver in a sharp, cutting wind by that gate. Harriet urges a run round the garden to get warm again. Mamma has begged them not to stand still in such cold. Young readers get a crisp Christmas scene of waiting, hope, and home rules.
20221-northern-nut-growers-association-r:
Northern Nut Growers Association reports record yearly meetings of growers and experts. This volume lists members from Nebraska to Ohio and beyond. William Caha of Wahoo and Ward M. Canaday of Toledo appear. Arthur S. Colby of the University of Illinois is also listed.

Such rolls show a wide, keen network behind American nut growing. Reports held talks, elections, and notes on trees and yields as well. Their value now lies in names, places, and dated facts. Readers tracing farm history or family names may find gold here. Growers shared seed, grafts, and hard-won lessons through these yearly gatherings.
20532-love-among-the-chickens-a-story-of:
P. G. Wodehouse published Love Among the Chickens in 1908, subtitled a story of the haps and mishaps on an English chicken farm. The narrator, Jeremy Garnet, is dragged down to Devon by his friend Ukridge. Ukridge plans to make a fortune raising chickens, a subject he knows nothing about.

Garnet reports the scheme's collapse with dry alarm. It is highly improbable, he says, that Ukridge will ever grow old if he repeats his last night's performance. The book mixes farm chaos with a love affair, in the comic style that soon made Wodehouse famous.
20851-character-sketches-of-romance-fict:
Mark Tapley, jolly through every hardship in Martin Chuzzlewit, stars in one sketch here. Dickens's man finds no credit in cheer when life runs smooth. Fever, fraud, and loss in Eden test his creed to the full.

Character Sketches of Romance, Fiction, and the Drama gathers famed figures in short accounts. E. B. Brewer's Reader's Handbook stands behind this vast, handy set. Volume three runs through plays, poems, and novels in alphabetical order. Readers once kept such sets by the desk to place a name or trace a tale in seconds.
20903-northern-nut-growers-association-r:
Connecticut names lead the roll in the Northern Nut Growers Association report. Tree experts, doctors, and growers from Stamford to Hartford fill the list. Their meeting papers treat the nuts that thrive in northern soils.

Chestnut, walnut, hickory, and filbert culture fills reports like this one in full detail. Growers swap notes on blight, grafts, soil, and yields by state. The group pushed nut trees as farm crops and shade plantings alike. These proceedings keep the craft of a niche farming world, exact and earnest, for growers and tree lovers to mine.
20915-field-s-chromatography-or-treatise:
Fresh hues on the walls of Theban tombs prove how old the science of colour runs. Field's Chromatography, a treatise on colours and pigments, opens with that deep past. Royal tomb paintings stayed so fresh, it says, as to need no repair.

George Field spent his life on pigments that would not fade or turn. Artists' colours, their making, and their faults fill his famed guide. Later editors rewrote and updated it for new generations of painters. The book stands as a bridge of craft, where chemistry serves art in the studio, colour by tested colour.
20938-stops-or-how-to-punctuate-a-practi:
Commas do too much work, charges Paul Allardyce in Stops, or How to Punctuate. Their vague use, he says, truly harms English style in our time. A firmer system for the old marks would pay at once, he argues.

Allardyce sets out each stop's right work in a practical handbook for writers. Comma, colon, dash, and full stop each get rules and cases. Students and clerks of the pen stood to gain most from its order. The book shows an age that prized clear prose taking its smallest tools with full gravity, mark by mark.
21190-expositions-of-holy-scripture-seco:
Alexander Maclaren, the great Manchester preacher, expounds six New Testament letters in this volume of his Expositions of Holy Scripture. It covers the end of Second Corinthians, Galatians, and Philippians in full, then Colossians, Thessalonians, and First Timothy. Each sermon takes a short text and opens it up.

Titles like Hope and Holiness, Rich Yet Poor, and Strength in Weakness show Maclaren's method. He takes a verse, gives a clear outline, and applies it closely to daily Christian life. He answers the charge that professing Christians often ignore common morality. These printed sermons let readers far from his pulpit study his preaching week by week.
21516-northern-nut-growers-association-r:
Growers of nut trees report their results in the Northern Nut Growers Association's printed proceedings. The reports carry the findings of each writer alone, not the backing of the group. A note warns that spray laws and advice may have changed since the papers were written.

Pages treat named kinds of nut trees, grafting, planting, and yields by district. A photo shows a Detroit grower standing under a fine tree, thanks to Gilbert Becker of Michigan. Members swap what worked in one soil and season, with no promise it will work elsewhere. For orchard keepers in cold states, the volume is a trove of trials.
21620-the-myth-of-hiawatha-and-other-ora:
Henry R. Schoolcraft gathers Indigenous tales in The Myth of Hiawatha, published at Philadelphia in 1856. He took the legends from the storytelling circle of the native wigwams. The book is dedicated to Longfellow, whose poem Hiawatha had just drawn on the same store.

Schoolcraft claims the tales show their tellers as they truly are. They reveal what the people believe, hope, fear, wish for, and worship. He argues they place Indigenous character in a wholly new light. As agent and scholar, Schoolcraft spent years among the Ojibwe and others, and his set remains a key, if dated, record.
21829-a-treatise-on-domestic-economy-for:
Running a home is a serious science in Catharine E. Beecher's Treatise on Domestic Economy, first issued in the 1840s for young ladies at home and school. Beecher blames poor health, poor servants, and faulty training for the wives whose strength failed in their first married years. Her book answers with method: health, order, and skill applied to every room of the house.

Chapters teach the care of health, food, children, servants, and the house itself, with engravings to guide the eye. Beecher dedicated the work to American mothers. It became one of the most used housekeeping books of its century. Modern readers find in it both practical lore and a clear window on women's work in 1845.
22094-travels-in-the-great-desert-of-sah:
James Richardson, an English traveller sent to open trade with the Sahara, crossed the great desert in 1845 and 1846. His Travels in the Great Desert of Sahara reports the journey from Tripoli toward the Sudan. Richardson apologises in his preface for the delayed map and commercial reports. The routes he surveyed were meant to guide British trade into the African interior.

He describes wells, caravans, Tuareg and Arab tribes, slavery, and the price of goods. The desert itself, its heat, sand, and thirst, dominates every chapter. Richardson later died on a second, grander expedition. His travels remain a basic source for the Sahara as Europeans first mapped it.
22200-recollections-with-photogravure-po:
David Christie Murray, a popular Victorian novelist, published his Recollections late in his career. The volume carries his portrait in photogravure and a preface of addresses. Murray begins with his birth on the thirteenth of April, which his mother called the unlucky day of the fool's month. He jokes that the phrase proved rich in prophetic wisdom about his life.

From a Birmingham childhood he rose through journalism to the London literary world. The Recollections roam over editors, actors, publishers, and the making of novels. Murray writes easily, with a professional's store of anecdote. His memoir is a useful, genial witness to the book trade of the late nineteenth century.
22238-charles-carleton-coffin-war-corres:
Charles Carleton Coffin was a Civil War correspondent, traveller, and author of boys' histories. This biography, published in 1898 near the end of his life, adds statesman to his titles. Its introduction says Coffin had a face that helped one believe in God. His whole life, the writer claims, was an evidence of Christianity, and he was an organiser of happiness who never sought riches.

Coffin reported Bull Run and a dozen other battles for Boston papers. Later his histories taught two generations of American boys their country's story. This life, written in warm admiration, records the reputation he left: the genial war correspondent who made history read like a story.
22260-bell-s-cathedrals-the-abbey-church:
H. J. L. J. Massé wrote this guide to Tewkesbury Abbey for Bell's Cathedral series. The little books in that series put a scholarly guide into a tourist's pocket. Massé thanks the owners of the Registrum Theokusburiae, the abbey's own register, for lending it for months. He also borrows plates on Saxon churches from the Archaeological Institute's journal, with leave.

Tewkesbury's great Norman tower and its tombs of princes fill the chapters. Massé traces the abbey from its founding through the Dissolution, when the townspeople bought their church to save it. The guide mixes architecture, history, and practical visiting notes. It is a model of the Edwardian church handbook.
22312-northern-nut-growers-association-r:
Growers who raised nut trees formed their own association and printed its proceedings. The Northern Nut Growers Association report records one such meeting. Its pages list members and officers by state and town.

The roll runs from Connecticut and Florida to Illinois, Indiana, and Ohio. Names appear from Panama's Canal Zone as well as Virginia and New York. That spread shows a young industry organizing itself across the country. Inside, readers find the working record of people trading knowledge on nut growing. It preserves names, places, and concerns of early American nut culture that would else be lost.
22400-fox-s-book-of-martyrs-or-a-history:
Fox's Book of Martyrs records the lives, sufferings, and deaths of Christian martyrs. John Foxe's great work stood in English homes beside the Bible for centuries. This edition carries his history of persecution onward.

Its preface argues that persecution is no one creed's vice. Intolerant Jew and bigoted pagan show the same spirit, it says. So do the nominal Christian, the infidel, and the atheist. The urge to force belief is called an inherent vice of fallen nature. Men try to restrain hated opinions by physical pressure. They use the same pressure to spread favored ones. The accounts that follow test that claim in blood.
22460-new-york-times-current-history-the:
The New York Times Current History gathered war news into monthly volumes. Volume two, number five, covers the European War in early 1915. Its pages reprint official notices and reports as they arrived.

On February 4, the German Admiralty proclaimed a war zone. Every enemy merchant ship found around Great Britain would be destroyed. It would not always be possible, Germany warned, to save crews. Passengers, too, would face dangers that could not be averted. That chilling notice marked a turn toward submarine warfare without mercy. Readers today get the war as Americans first read it. It is history in the raw, before outcomes were known.
22471-the-fair-play-settlers-of-the-west:
George D. Wolf studied the Fair Play settlers of the West Branch Valley. Their years, 1769 to 1784, frame his study of frontier ethnography. These settlers governed themselves beyond Pennsylvania's official reach and law.

Wolf calls their story worth telling for one clear reason. It might offer insight into democracy's development on the frontier. His account is an ethnography of how these settlers lived and ruled. He warns it is not meant to typify all frontiers. It is simply an illustration, and he hopes a useful one. Readers get a close case study in self-government. Settlers made law where no law had been provided for them.
22589-jubilation-u-s-a:
Jubilation, U.S.A. is a science fiction story about alien visitors arriving in a very ordinary America. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. In the sample scene, two aliens halt on a road as a wheezing pre-war Chevy chokes its way toward them.

The visitors step into a gully beside the road, ready to run for their ship if the welcome turns hostile. They expect a friendly reception, but they are not sure of their figures. That mix of cosmic travel and small-town caution gives the story its dry comic tone. It belongs to the magazine tradition that played first contact for gentle satire rather than terror. Readers of classic short science fiction will enjoy its deadpan setup.
22721-northern-nut-growers-association-r:
The Northern Nut Growers Association Report of the Proceedings is a conference record from the society that promoted nut growing in northern North America. The catalog record names no editor and gives no year. Papers, discussions, and membership lists make up the volume, as in the association's other reports.

The surviving sample is a roll of members and contacts, state by state: Alabama, Alberta, British Columbia, California, Connecticut, and on through Manitoba, Mexico, and the New England states. Names like Dr. Colt in California and A. Hale in Alberta mark a network of growers swapping varieties and results. Proceedings of this kind carried the practical science of a niche crop. Orchard historians can trace from them how northern nut culture spread.
22831-as-a-chinaman-saw-us-passages-from:
America gets reviewed by a visitor in As a Chinaman Saw Us, a set of letters home from a Chinese traveler. He writes with dry care. The great powers, he notes, believe they are still evolving toward perfection, while Americans assure him the United States has already arrived. Criticizing such a finished nation, he jokes, takes real nerve.

That polite irony runs through the letters. Customs, manners, politics, and national pride all pass before a calm outsider's eye, and his praise often carries a sting. The book belongs to a small shelf of works that reversed the usual travel gaze of the period. It still reads freshly because its main tool, understatement, has not dated at all.
australian-legendary-tales-folk-lore-of-: Katie Langloh Parker's Australian Legendary Tales preserves the folklore of the Noongahburrah people. The ancient legends tell of creation, clever animals, and powerful spirits of the bush. These were among the very first Aboriginal tales ever set down in print. A precious and irreplaceable record of an ancient living culture.
chimes-of-mission-bells-an-historical-sk: Maria Antonia Field sketches the history of California's missions — their founding by Franciscan padres, their Indigenous converts, and their romantic ruins. Written with affection for the Spanish past, the book preserves the lore of old California. A gentle, nostalgic history of the mission era.

fiat-money-inflation-in-france-how-it-ca: Andrew Dickson White — founder of Cornell University — traces France's disastrous experiment with paper money during the Revolution. godliness-being-reports-of-a-series-of-a: Catherine Booth — the Mother of the Salvation Army — delivered these powerful addresses on holy living to crowded London halls. good-stories-for-great-holidays-arranged: This collection arranges holiday stories for telling aloud. Seasons gather. The Tower library holds the full text. It storied holidays. Voices read. govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Afro-AmericanCi: A UPI clipping from Los Angeles, dated October 10, reports a surprise endorsement from the 1968 presidential campaign. govdocs-archive_org-nsia-AutopsyJFKParkl: C. J. Price was the administrator of Parkland Memorial Hospital in Dallas, where President Kennedy died, and he gave one of the earliest statements on the hospital's part in the day. The papers filed under his name, on the Kennedy case and Parkland, make up this file. It is kept as issued, part of the Dallas hospital record that researchers still use beside the Warren Commission exhibits.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BarbeeWilliamA_: William Barbee's name heads a declassified US government file held by the Internet Archive. The catalog gives no date, no agency, no hint of contents - just the name and the govdocs tag. No public text has surfaced. A bare named record for those tracing declassified files.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BushGeorge_Busc:
In the days after President Kennedy's assassination, the State Department worried about what armed anti-Castro exiles might do next. This memorandum warned that such groups might exploit the situation to mount unauthorized raids against Cuba, and it was distributed to United States intelligence agencies.

A raid in that charged moment could have wrecked American policy and inflamed the hemisphere, so the warning went out through official channels; the memo rests in FBI file 62-104060. The document shows the government's fear that private armies might act while the nation was in shock. It is Cold War paperwork with the tension of that winter still on it.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-EisenbergMelvin:
Melvin A. Eisenberg, a Warren Commission staff lawyer, wrote a memorandum on April 22, 1964 about a conference on the Zapruder film. Pathologists, wound-ballistics experts, and commission staff had met to study the film frame by frame. Their task was precise: find the frames that show the instants the first and second bullets struck.

Pinning shots to frames let the commission match the film to the wounds and build its timeline of the shooting. Eisenberg's summary records how the experts reasoned their way to those frames. It is a working paper from inside the inquiry, written while the final report was still being shaped.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FerrellHubertAB:
An FBI document dated April 12, 1968 concerns Hubert A. Buck Ferrell. Ferrell reported a warning from an informant: an unnamed they had tried to get Martin Luther King two weeks before he was killed. The informant said they would try again, and King was shot on April 4.

The document was written eight days after the assassination, when every warning looked different in hindsight. A claim of an earlier attempt raised hard questions about what was known and passed on. The Bureau recorded Ferrell's report in the flood of paper the King investigation produced.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FrazierRobertA_:
The day after the assassination, the FBI Laboratory sent a report to Dallas Police Chief Jesse E. Curry. Dated November 23, 1963, the report covers the laboratory's examination of assassination evidence. Dallas police held the crime scene and the suspect, while the Bureau's lab in Washington did the scientific work.

Lab findings on bullets, fragments, and weapons became the physical spine of the case. A report issued within a day shows how fast that work began. It preserves the first formal link between the Dallas investigation and the federal laboratory studying its evidence.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-IntelligenceAge:
Historian Robert Dallek reviewed Christopher Andrew's book Secret Intelligence and the American Presidency, published by HarperCollins. Andrew's history runs through the CIA, the FBI, the NSA, and the National Security Council. Dallek, a presidential historian, judges the book from his own field.

Presidents are the customers of secret intelligence, and Andrew wrote the agencies' story from the Oval Office outward. A review by Dallek weighs how well that story is told. The piece preserves two historians meeting on the ground where secrecy and power overlap, and it gives general readers a guided way into Andrew's long book.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-McKenzieWilliam:
The FBI's Dallas office sent this teletype to the Director on March 5, 1964. Its subject was William A. McKenzie, the attorney for Marina Oswald and for Robert Oswald, the accused assassin's widow and brother. McKenzie said that information in a Dallas airtel was for the bureau's eyes only.

Teletypes were the bureau's urgent traffic, and this one concerns control of information. A lawyer for the two people closest to Oswald was dealing directly with agents, while the Warren Commission worked. The message preserves the tension in a single line: the bureau held material about the Oswalds that their own lawyer insisted stay inside the bureau.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-RemingtonRogerA: A fragment of Warren Commission testimony survives here, without its full context. Representatives Gerald Ford and John McCloy question a witness about Dr. Malcolm Perry's examination of Governor Connally's wounds. Perry treated both Kennedy and Connally at Parkland Hospital. The fragment preserves an exchange about the governor's wounds and the doctors who probed them. The witness's identity and the hearing's full setting are not recoverable from the fragment alone.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-SneedLarryA_Sne: nsia-SneedLarryA Sneed Larry A: the made public government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, complete. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WardAndPaulRepo: Ward and Paul Reporting Services billed the Warren Commission for its work, and the invoices survive. Court reporters took down the commission's testimony word for word in 1964. Their billing records show the business side of a famous investigation: hours worked, pages produced, and charges sent to the government. Few readers see invoices, but they prove how much labor a public inquiry quietly consumed.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-YardumHarryA_Ya: Harry Yardum sent Harold Weisberg a postcard with a simple question: was he still working on the assassination case? Postcards were the quick notes of their day, and researchers traded many of them. Yardum's card shows readers checking on Weisberg's progress and morale. The answer, as his files show, was yes for the rest of his life.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_chile_CH:
Fifty years after Chile's military coup of September 11, 1973, the National Security Archive marked the anniversary with declassified records. Countdown Toward a Coup follows the long road to that day, step by step.

A countdown format suits the story well, because the coup had a long approach: an election Washington tried to block, a government it worked to strangle, and generals it quietly encouraged. The briefing book's documents let readers watch the pieces move into place over three years. For the fiftieth anniversary, the Archive chose paper over speeches, publishing the record of how a democracy was brought down.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_chile_Th:
Michael Townley was an American operative who worked for DINA, the secret police of Chile's Pinochet dictatorship. His papers and confessions form the core of this briefing book, number 847, published in November 2023. Peter Kornbluh and John Dinges edited it for the fiftieth anniversary of DINA's creation.

Townley's secret admissions describe DINA's part in state-sponsored terrorism under the military regime. They cover supplying nerve gas used to murder Chileans, an Operation Condor mission in France, and the Letelier-Moffitt assassination in Washington. Few records put an insider's own account of these crimes in one place.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_chile_Judge_Juan_:
Juan Guzman Tapia was the first Chilean judge to prosecute Augusto Pinochet for human rights crimes, a step no court in Chile had dared before him. When Guzman died, the National Security Archive published this tribute in January 2021, remembering him as a figure of justice, truth, and dignity.

Pinochet ruled Chile from 1973 to 1990, and his regime tortured and killed thousands. Guzman's cases used the regime's own disappearances against him, treating each kidnapping as a crime still open while the victim stayed missing. That legal path changed what accountability could look like in Chile. The tribute gives readers a short, clear account of one judge's role in bringing a former dictator within reach of the law.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_foia_The_Capitol_:
What happened at the Capitol on January 6, 2021 has been told by official testimony, by news reporting, and by the Pentagon, and the three do not fully agree. The National Security Archive built a timeline that pieces the day's events together, and this posting presents that chronology and the gaps it reveals.

The Archive highlights unresolved differences between sworn testimony, media accounts, and the Defense Department's own sparse timeline. A chronology sounds like a simple thing, but here it works as an audit. Hour by hour, claim by claim, it shows where the record is firm and where it still breaks down. Readers who want the day's sequence separated from argument, with the disputed points marked honestly, are the audience for this piece.
hume-history-of-england-1860-part-a:
David Hume, the Scottish philosopher, wrote his History of England between 1754 and 1762 and remade his fame with it. Part A here opens the 1860 Virtue edition, which spreads the work across three volumes in six parts. The history runs from Julius Caesar's landing to the Glorious Revolution of 1688, in seventy-one chapters.

Hume wrote with a philosopher's calm, weighing kings and parties without the rage of his age. His smooth, clear prose made the book the standard history of England for a hundred years. Readers trusted his fairness even when they fought his views on religion. Part A begins that long, balanced march through the island's past.
jean-of-the-lazy-a: A Western romance by B. M. Bower, one of the first women to make a career writing cowboy fiction, set on a Montana cattle ranch. It follows Jean, a spirited ranch girl, through rustlers, range feuds, and a slow-burning love story. Bower knew real ranch life, and her books brought an authenticity and a woman's viewpoint rare in early Westerns.
john-smith-u-s-a:
John Smith, U.S.A. is a book of poetry and prose by Eugene Field, issued in 1905. Its introduction praises Field as a poet of keen perception and rare judgment. It also calls him a humorist as delicate as Artemus Ward, Mark Twain, or Bret Harte. Field was best loved for his verse for children, yet he often left that world to write for older readers.

The introducer knew Field slightly, through the same city, college, and newspaper work in St. Louis and Chicago. He argues that the world is better for Field's life, not in gold but in priceless truths. The title poem gives the book its patriotic name. Readers meet Field the whimsical newsman-poet, whose Temple of Mirth the introduction invites them to enter.
legends-traditions-and-laws-of-the-iroqu:
Elias Johnson, a native Tuscarora chief, wrote this history of the Iroquois. Its full title adds a history of the Tuscarora Indians. Editors warn that his English may seem strange to some readers.

Johnson wrote in a language not his first, they explain. He records legends, traditions, and laws of the Six Nations. His own people's story receives special, detailed treatment. Few books of his era gave an Indigenous author this platform. His work preserves Iroquois self-history from inside the confederacy. A history of the Tuscarora fills the book's second half. Johnson signs himself a chief of that nation proudly.
lighted-to-lighten-the-hope-of-india-a-s:
Alice B. Van Doren studied conditions among India's women for this 1922 book. A central committee recommended it for women's society programs. They found it less difficult and more concrete than Fleming's study. Illustrations show colleges, temples, and village homes in India.

One pictured girl, Meenachi of Madura, was married to a god. Another, Arul, knew a very different sort of home. Regina Thumboo College at Lucknow produced its first M.A. graduate. The book asks what life will bring to India's daughters. Priests of a Hindu temple appear among the listed illustrations. What will life bring to her, the captions ask repeatedly.
literary-friends-and-acquaintance-a-pers:
William Dean Howells looks back over American authorship he knew personally. Contents move from his first New England visit onward. Literary Boston, Cambridge neighbors, and New York impressions fill chapters. Portraits of Holmes, Longfellow, Lowell, and Mark Twain close the list.

Howells says he meant for years to write these papers. Daily meetings with great writers went unrecorded at the time. His memory, though retentive, supplied less than he wished. Still he trusts his impressions stayed honest and accurate. Ten years of desultory writing produced these papers, he confesses. First impressions of literary New York precede the Boston chapters.
memoirs-of-the-court-of-st-cloud-being-s:
Lewis Goldsmith wrote the Memoirs of the Court of St. Cloud as secret letters. A gentleman at Paris writes to a nobleman in London, the title says. A publishers' note promises facts on Napoleon found in no other book.

The letter writer, said to be Stewarton, knew Josephine in her glad days. He gives lives of near all Napoleon's ministers and generals. Royalists who crossed over stand beside men risen by war. Odd vanishings of folk who irked Napoleon get stark tales here. Talleyrand and Fouche stand among the famed names in its tales. Court life from inside, not from gazettes, is its promise.
myths-and-legends-of-our-own-land-volume:
Charles M. Skinner gives the heartland its own volume of legends here. Saint Clair's obstinacy and the Black Swamp crime open the list. Marquette's man-eater and a coffin of snakes raise the stakes. Lake Superior's water gods rule the northern tales.

Were-wolves of Detroit and the Nain Rouge prowl the contents. Hiawatha, Pipestone, and the Falls of St. Anthony add Native lore. French voyageurs left tales along these lakes and rivers. Frontier ghosts walk beside them in Skinner's telling. The volume proves the Midwest holds folklore as rich and strange as any seacoast in the Union.
nasa-tm-19650005989-a-dichroic-subreflec:
Robert L Hensell and Paul A Lantz at Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this December 1964 paper on a special antenna mirror. A Cassegrain antenna uses a small second mirror, called a subreflector, in front of a large main dish. Their subreflector is dichroic, meaning it treats different signals differently.

Their design lets the main dish also be fed at its prime focus. In effect, one antenna can work in two ways instead of one. That saves size and weight on a ground or space antenna. The paper gives engineers a concrete way to get that dual use.
nasa-tm-19650023903-the-screening-effect:
H Martinides, a European Space Research Organization member who worked at Goddard for a year, wrote this study on January 5, 1965. When waves meet a straight-edged obstacle, part of the space behind it falls in shadow. The edge also bends the waves, an effect called diffraction. Martinides treats that screening problem with mathematics.

His contents move from the classic treatment to two named diffraction methods. The half-plane is the model obstacle in the study. Such problems arise in optics, radio work, and antenna design. A clean solution for a straight edge gives engineers a base case, against which real screens and shields can be judged.
nasa-tm-19650025661-hypoxemia-induced-by:
W C Alexander of the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston, with R J Sever and F G Hoppin of the Naval Air Development Center, studied a hidden risk of hard acceleration. Pilots breathing pure oxygen at low pressure can still suffer low oxygen in the blood. The condition is called hypoxemia. Sustained forward acceleration was the trigger under study.

The test setting copied a spacecraft cabin, at five pounds per square inch of pure oxygen. Even there, acceleration could reduce oxygen uptake. That finding mattered for launch and reentry profiles in crewed flight. The study joins flight medicine with vehicle design, showing a case where more oxygen in the cabin did not settle the problem.
nasa-tm-19670009071-static-aerodynamic-c:
Eugene N. Brooks Jr., John P. Decker, and James A. Blackwell Jr., of NASA's Langley Research Center in Virginia, wrote this memorandum, issued in February 1967. Numbered TM X-1345, it reports wind-tunnel measurements on a model of a typical subsonic, swept-wing jet transport. NASA wanted handling data for recovering such airplanes from steep attitudes and near-sonic speeds in rough air.

Tests in Langley's 8-foot transonic pressure tunnel covered speeds from Mach 0.40 to Mach 1.20. Angles of attack ran from minus eight to eighteen degrees. At modest lift, the model stayed longitudinally stable across the whole speed range. Above Mach 0.90, its static margin grew sharply with small speed changes. At higher lift the margin shrank toward zero at lower speeds. Sideways stability also flipped sign near Mach 0.90, though weathercock stability held throughout.
nasa-tm-19670013990-solar-and-geomagneti:
S. Chandra and B. V. Krishnamurthy, of the Laboratory for Space Sciences at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this paper in March 1967. It studies what heats the upper atmosphere. That thin region swells and shrinks with solar activity, changing the drag on satellites that pass through it.

Solar extreme ultraviolet radiation is widely accepted as one major heat source, the authors note. Whether particle, or corpuscular, radiation adds a second source of similar size was sharply disputed. Most temperature evidence came indirectly, from satellite drag measurements that yield air density at a satellite's lowest point. Model atmospheres then convert density into an exospheric temperature. To test the two candidate heat sources, the study compares those temperatures against solar radio flux measures and day-to-day geomagnetic variation.
nasa-tm-19670022197-design-and-experimen:
George W. Lewis, Edward R. Tysl, and Melvin J. Hartmann, of NASA's Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, wrote this memorandum in September 1960. It reports the design and test of a small centrifugal pump for liquid hydrogen. Liquid hydrogen is extremely cold and thin, so pumping it without flow problems is hard.

The authors expect such pumps to use large diameter ratios and many splitter blades. They designed a small pump using a method adapted from centrifugal-compressor practice. The design produced the passage and blade shapes and the blade count and positions. In tests, the shrouded rotor's performance was relatively good for its class.
nasa-tm-19670030005-mathematical-relatio:
Issued by NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, this paper treats antenna geometry for the manned space flight tracking network. It gives the mathematical relationships of the MFOD antenna axes. Tracking antennas in the United States used three different primary coordinate systems. A station's fix on a spacecraft also needed slant range to be complete.

The three systems are azimuth-elevation, X-Y, and hour angle-declination mounts. Each has particular advantages and disadvantages, which the report tabulates side by side. An azimuth-elevation mount, for example, can lose an overhead pass because its azimuth rate peaks at the zenith. An X-Y mount, by contrast, tracks straight through the zenith. Many remote network sites had equipment of two different types sitting side by side. Pointing data then had to move between systems, so the report develops all the equations required to interrelate position data among the three.
nasa-tm-19680021590-brayton-cycle-altern:
M. G. Kofskey, W. J. Nusbaum, and W. L. Stewart of Lewis Research Center wrote this 1968 paper, TM X-52430, for an energy conversion conference in Boulder, Colorado. Their subject is the small turbine that drives the alternator in a Brayton cycle space power system. In the reference design, one turbine drives the compressor and a second drives the alternator.

Tests of the two-stage turbine showed a satisfactory level of efficiency, in the authors' words. Clearance at the rotor tips mattered a great deal, while flow speed effects stayed small. Applied to the full system, the turbine ran one point above its design efficiency. Its performance also held steady across a wide range of power output.
nasa-tm-19690028981-round-trip-trajector:
E. A. Willis Jr. and J. A. Padrutt of Lewis Research Center study round trips stopping at both Mars and Venus in this 1969 memorandum. The trajectories enter parking orbits at both planets before returning to Earth. Such combined trips sit between classic opposition-class and conjunction-class Mars missions in effort, time, and stay.

Using a two-body, impulsive trajectory model, the authors compare mission options. Propulsive effort and trip times for the combined stopover trips need not be greatly higher than for Mars or Venus alone. In any case, those totals stay below running separate trips to each planet. The study maps an efficient way to visit two planets in one expedition.
nasa-tm-19700009929-electromagnetic-perf:
Gary Bollenbacher and Heinz L. Wimmer of the Lewis Research Center tested a 1200-hertz Lundell alternator built for a Brayton-cycle power system. Such a system was meant to make electric power for spacecraft. Their question was plain: how much power could the machine give before its own magnetism set the limit?

Overload tests pushed the machine, rated near eleven kilowatts, well past that mark, though hard heating kept each run short. Output reached twenty-six kilowatts at one setting and forty-four kilowatts at another, as the summary states. From lower-power data the authors estimate top efficiency near eighty-eight percent. The results helped set a fair rating for an improved system and its cooling needs.
nasa-tm-19700015967-the-characteristics-:
David W. Jex, Archie M. Miller, and Charles A. MacKay of the Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this report on January 5, 1970. It studies how well a two-sheet structure with a honeycomb core resists being punched through. Walls of this sandwich kind were candidates for spacecraft skins.

Fast particles and debris can strike a craft in orbit and pierce weak walls. The report gives the penetration traits of the double-sheet honeycomb design under such hits. Results of this kind helped engineers judge how much protection a wall gives. They could then pick wall designs that keep crews and equipment safe.
nasa-tm-19700016378-evaluation-of-a-flui:
Milton J. LeRoy Jr. and Sol H. Gorland of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a 1970 metrology conference in Washington. It evaluates a fluidic oscillator as a sensor of gas molecular weight. The device switches a gas jet back and forth with no moving parts.

The switching rate of the jet depends on the gas passing through it. That link lets the device report the weight of gas molecules, a clue to which gas is present. The paper judges how well the sensor does this job. Work of this kind served plants and craft that must track gas mixtures safely.
nasa-tm-19700022616-smooth-empirical-bay:
Kemble Bennett of the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston wrote this study, issued in June 1970. It began as his doctoral dissertation at Texas Tech University. The subject is smooth empirical Bayes estimation, a way to estimate unknowns from mixed data.

Bennett applies his method to the Weibull distribution. That distribution is a workhorse for predicting how long parts last before they fail. Better estimates of its shape mean better life forecasts for hardware. A space agency that must trust parts for years has strong use for such methods. The work links abstract statistics to plain questions of reliability.
nasa-tm-19700025468-manual-for-operation:
The Design Engineering Directorate at the Kennedy Space Center issued this manual on May 21, 1969. It tells how to run the center's automatic pipe and tube welding machine. The machine covered is the APW-3, in its modified form, under document number GP-630.

The manual opens with an introduction that states its purpose and scope. It then gives a working description of the machine and what each part does. Welds on pipes and tubes had to be sound for fuel and gas lines at the launch site. A clear shop manual helped operators make the same good weld every time.
nasa-tm-19710005442-a-method-of-describi:
Michio Aoyagi of the Ames Research Center wrote this study of nerve cell firing. It gives a method for describing the spontaneous activity of nerve units. After each impulse, such a unit rests for a dead time that varies by chance.

Aoyagi models the pattern of gaps between the unit's spikes. His method rests on a picture of nerve behavior put forward by Harris and Flock. It works out the possible shapes of the gap pattern that picture allows. In an appendix, he applies the method to a real record. The record came from a single vestibular nerve unit taken from a frog.
nasa-tm-19710008663-unstart-and-stall-in:
David A Choby, Paul L Burstadt, and James E Calogeras of the Lewis Research Center wrote this March 1971 technical memorandum, NASA TM X-2192. It studies what happens when a supersonic inlet suddenly stops working well, an event called unstart. The test paired a turbojet engine with a round inlet that squeezed the air by sixty percent.

Tests ran in the Lewis ten by ten foot supersonic wind tunnel. At Mach 1.98, the pressure ratio that stalled the engine during unstart matched the steady stall value. At Mach 2.50, the unstart shock was so strong that it stalled the compressor at every setting. Back pressuring the engine also sent hammer shocks through the inlet. Those shocks pushed wall pressures above the free stream total pressure.
nasa-tm-19710013720-prediction-of-the-th:
R C Hendricks and A Baron of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for an August 1971 heat transfer meeting in Tulsa. It predicts a sharp rise, called an anomaly, in how well simple fluids carry heat near their critical point. The critical region is where liquid and gas states blur together. Engineers need those values for design work.

The team studied five gases, from carbon dioxide to methane. Their method joined an existing theory with a known equation of state. The analysis matched the trend of measured data well. Results ran somewhat high at the greatest densities. The authors judged the method sound for engineering use and for fluids lacking data.
nasa-tm-19710014580-adiabatic-invariance:
David P. Stern of the Goddard Space Flight Center delivered this lecture at the University of Wisconsin in Milwaukee on April 21, 1971. His subject is adiabatic invariance, the idea that some quantities stay nearly fixed while a system changes very slowly. Stern presents the talk as a case history of how one physics concept evolved.

He notes the idea's odd path: it began with a quantum problem and ended up in classical mechanics. The story starts around 1900, when physicists were surprised that radiation gave up its energy only in discrete amounts. Stern follows the concept through radiation studies and the mechanics of moving bodies. He closes by stressing that the story is unfinished, with unresolved problems and unexplored avenues still open.
nasa-tm-19710069675-postflight-evaluatio:
Postflight Evaluation of Atlas-Centaur AC-3 is a May 1965 report by the staff of the Lewis Research Center, issued as NASA TM X-1094. AC-3 launched on June 30, 1964, early in the Atlas-Centaur program. Postflight evaluations check how every stage and system actually behaved during a launch, so lessons can feed fixes into the next vehicle.

The contents move system by system. A trajectory section compares the Atlas and Centaur flight phases and reconstructs the path, including Centaur specific impulse worked out two ways. Propulsion sections cover Atlas and Centaur performance, startup and cutoff behavior, boost pumps, main pumps, and hydraulic and peroxide systems. Later sections treat Centaur propellant systems, tank pressurization, hydrogen venting, and the pressures and temperatures around the nose fairing.
new-york-times-current-history-the-europ:
April 1915 opens volume two of the New York Times Current History of the European War. The Times Company published the monthly in New York, with an index for April to September. Its first item takes up Germany's war zone and neutral flags.

The German decree and an exchange of notes on the decree lead the number. A piece on Germany's submarine war follows, with a map. Karl Lamprecht argues that the German people are not blinded. A poem called Reveille sits among the reports. Neutral rights at sea, and the new submarine threat, dominate this early 1915 number for American readers.
northern-nut-growers-association-report-:
Growers in the Northern Nut Growers Association met at Rochester, New York, on September 1 and 2, 1915, for their sixth annual meeting. This book reports the proceedings of that meeting. Papers by members make up the report. A modern disclaimer at the front speaks for the association's reports as a set.

That notice says each article gives its author's own findings and thoughts, not the group's backing. It warns that pesticide laws and advice have changed since the pieces were written. Talks name specific nut tree kinds and ways of growing them. What worked in one place and season, the notice adds, may not work elsewhere. Orchard keepers were the first readers.
notes-and-queries-index-of-volume-1-nove:
Notes and Queries called itself a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. Its motto, from Captain Cuttle, ran: when found, make a note of. This file holds the index to volume one, which ran from November 1849 to May 1850. Entries run by letter, with page numbers.

Under A alone sit the Abbey of St Wandrille and the abdication of James the Second. Aboriginal chambers near Tilbury and Aelfric's colloquy appear nearby. Metrical writings on alchemy and King Alfred's geography of Europe follow. The index lets a reader find any small query or answer in the volume. Such finding lists made the journal usable as a store of facts.
on-the-prospects-of-christianity-bernard:
Bernard Shaw wrote this preface in the year 1912. It introduces his play Androcles and the Lion. The contents ask why not give Christianity a trial. He asks if Jesus was a coward or a martyr. He treats the Gospels without prejudice, he claims.

Shaw separates atonement from mere punishment in his argument. He traces salvation from class privilege toward remedy. Luther and Calvin complete his scheme of the story. Long sections then read Matthew, Mark, and Luke closely. Shaw writes with wit, paradox, and provocation throughout. The preface is longer and bolder than the play.
peignot-essai-historique-sur-la-liberte-: In the hosted sample, only the title pages of Gabriel Peignot's Essai historique, in rough scanned type, with no chapter text visible. The title announces a historical essay on the freedom to write among the ancients and the moderns, and on the freedom of the press since the fifteenth century. It promises the means of repression used against those freedoms in all times. It adds many anecdotes and notes, a synoptic table of printing in France, and a chronology of press laws from 1789 to 1831.
podcast-dannyjones-mNghN4vMQ_A:
Bible scholar Dan McClellan joins Danny Jones to talk about the Dead Sea Scrolls, drugs in the ancient world, and Jesus Christ. McClellan is a scholar of the Bible and its tongues who posts short talks for a wide crowd.

McClellan explains what the scrolls truly say and where pop claims run past the proof. He weighs the case for drug use in old rites with a scholar's care. Jones asks the bold questions fans send in. Listeners get a pro's guide to hot claims, with the hype stripped off. The library holds the talk as an archive record.
podcast-joerogan-AJ0-VeWMr-A:
Actress Leah Remini joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 908 to talk about Scientology, the church she was raised in and later left. Remini became the most famous public critic of the group, with a memoir and a TV series built on former members' accounts.

She tells Rogan what life inside the church looked like, from its rules to the cost of leaving. Rogan asks about the stars the church courts and the stories ex-members share with her. The episode is a plain-spoken exposé, mixing one woman's escape story with a wider look at control and faith.
podcast-joerogan-KfW_rjccp-A:
Duncan Trussell's episode 2009 of the Joe Rogan Experience came just after the show's two-thousandth entry, and it keeps the party mood. Trussell, the comedian whose riffs mix psychedelics and philosophy, is the guest Rogan's audience treats as family. No topic is assigned; none is needed.

The pair drift through trips, gods, jokes, and the strange comfort of old friendship. Rogan plays the straight man when Trussell's tales lift off. The episode is not a lesson so much as a seat at the table, and it shows why this guest, of all guests, anchors the show's freewheeling side.
poncet-de-la-riviere-discours-du-magistr:
French readers of 1766 met a courtroom thunderbolt in this speech by a magistrate before the assembled chambers, dated April 10 of that year. The target is a pastoral instruction by the Bishop of Troyes on the schism. A publication the magistrate calls an attack on the peace the king's declaration of September 1754 was meant to restore in church and state. The speech calls the hunt for supposed differences of religion within the kingdom the surest way to foment discord among the faithful and, by consequence, among citizens.

In the old spelling of the period, the orator dissects the bishop's preface. Its claim that a private person reprinted the suppressed instruction, and its declamations against supposed attacks on dogma and sacraments. The document is Gallican France in action: royal courts policing bishops in the name of public peace, in the long Jansenist fight.
punch-or-the-london-charivari-volume-152: Front matter for volume 152 of Punch survives here on its own: a title page for the half-year volume and a calendar for 1917. The calendar sets out the year month by month in the paper's compact grid, weeks running from Sunday. January through March appear in full in the surviving pages. Readers get the volume's frame rather than its jokes: cover matter telling binder and reader exactly which run of the weekly sat between the boards.
robert-f-murray-author-of-the-scarlet-go: The poems of Robert F. Murray, the young Scottish poet who died at twenty-five, with a memoir of his brief life. His verses of student days and early promise charmed readers in the 1890s. A touching memorial to talent cut short.
st-patrick-s-day-or-the-scheming-lieuten: Richard Brinsley Sheridan — the great wit behind The School for Scandal — offers this brisk one-act farce of soldiers, sweethearts, and scheming. Written for a St. Patrick's Day benefit, it delivers mistaken identities and happy endings at top speed. A small, sparkling gem from the golden age of English comedy.
the-twin-hells-a-thrilling-narrative-of-: John N. Reynolds's 1890 firsthand account of hard life in Kansas and Missouri, written from personal experience of the region's roughest corners. Vivid and sensational, it documents a violent frontier era. A raw, unvarnished voice from the border wars' aftermath.
theatrum-chemicum-zetzner-1602-a:
Lazarus Zetzner, a Strasbourg printer, issued the first printing of the Theatrum Chemicum in 1602. He gathered key tracts by leading alchemical authors into one large set. For readers of the time, it became the central library of the art.

Inside are treatises on metals, furnaces, elixirs, and the search for deep change in matter. The authors mix craft skill, faith, and bold claims about nature's secrets. Later adepts treated the set as their canon of classic texts. This first printing matters because it fixed which old works would be read, copied, and trusted for the next hundred years.
un-ga-res-51-198-a:
Guatemala's rights mission had its term set in Resolution 51/198 A, passed in December 1996. The Mission for the Verification of Human Rights in Guatemala had been set up in 1994. An April 1996 vote had stretched its term by nine months and more, to the end of that year. The Assembly had the mission chief's fifth report before it.

That report weighs how the state of Guatemala and the rebel URNG kept their pledges under the rights deal. Its findings and counsel are taken note of in the text. The vote came days before the firm and lasting peace was signed at Guatemala City on 29 December 1996, ending a civil war of 36 years.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 51/198 A, adopted on 17 December 1996, renewed the Guatemala human rights verification mission until 31 March 1997. The Assembly noted the mission director's fifth report. It welcomed the government's steps against impunity. It took heart from a real halt in fighting, won through trust-building steps by both sides.

Peace had moved fast. Accords on economic and land questions had been signed. Accords on civilian power and the army's role in a democratic society had been signed. The final peace was set to be signed on 29 December 1996 in Guatemala City. The Secretary-General was asked for plans to reshape the mission for its new tasks after the signing.
